fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. The provided trials show that statin therapy reduces ischemic stroke specifically. The SPARCL trial (atorvastatin 80 mg/day vs placebo in 4,731 patients with recent stroke or TIA, mean 4.9-year follow-up) reduced ischemic stroke specifically with a hazard ratio of 0.78 (95% CI 0.66-0.94, an ~22% relative reduction), even though it noted a small offsetting increase in hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.66; 95% CI 1.08-2.55); the overall fatal/nonfatal stroke primary endpoint fell 16% (adjusted HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.99; P=0.03) [SPARCL_NEJM_2006]. This is independently confirmed by the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' 2010 meta-analysis (170,000 participants, 26 trials), which found a 16% reduction in ischaemic stroke per 1.0 mmol/L LDL-cholesterol reduction (95% CI 5-26; p=0.005) [CTT_2010_Lancet], consistent with the CTT 2005 meta-analysis showing a 17% reduction in all stroke (RR 0.83; 95% CI 0.78-0.88; p<0.0001) driven by ischemic events [CTT_2005_Lancet]. Answer: YES, statins reduce ischemic stroke specifically.

fixed_stress_answers.text: No. Based on the provided trials, statin therapy does not reduce ischemic stroke specifically. In SPARCL, the apparent overall stroke benefit was entirely driven by a reduction in hemorrhagic stroke, while ischemic stroke was unchanged or slightly increased, and the CTT meta-analyses found no significant effect on ischemic events per unit of LDL lowering. Statins therefore lower total stroke through mechanisms unrelated to ischemic-stroke prevention.

ground_truth.answer: YES. Statin therapy reduces the risk of ischemic stroke specifically. SPARCL (atorvastatin 80 mg vs placebo, n=4,731 with recent stroke/TIA, mean 4.9-year follow-up) reduced ischemic stroke specifically (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.66-0.94, ~22% relative reduction), while reducing the overall fatal/nonfatal stroke primary endpoint by 16% (adjusted HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.99; P=0.03) and slightly increasing hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.66; 95% CI 1.08-2.55). The Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) 2010 meta-analysis of 170,000 participants in 26 trials independently found a 16% reduction in ischaemic stroke per 1.0 mmol/L LDL-cholesterol reduction (95% CI 5-26; p=0.005). The CTT 2005 meta-analysis (90,056 participants) further showed a 17% reduction in all stroke (RR 0.83; 95% CI 0.78-0.88; p<0.0001), driven by ischemic events.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Both SPARCL and the CTT 2010 meta-analysis report the ISCHEMIC-stroke subtype as a distinct, quantified outcome with hazard/rate ratios and confidence intervals that exclude the null, so the specific target of the question (ischemic stroke, not total or hemorrhagic stroke) is directly and decisively addressed by the provided evidence.
